Niels Lyhne hastened back home. Alone among so many unknown faces, he could no longer endure being abroad. Yet as Copenhagen drew nearer, he asked himself more and more often what he expected to find there, and increasingly wished he had stayed away. Who was there for him in Copenhagen? Certainly not Frithjof. Erik, travelling through Italy on a scholarship, was absent too. Mrs. Boye? His connection with Mrs. Boye was a curious business. Coming directly from his mother's grave, he could not call it a profanation, precisely, or anything of that sort; yet it jarred against the pitch of his present feelings. It sounded a false note. Had he been returning to a fiancée, a youthful, blushing bride, that would have accorded with a heart occupied so long by a son's duties. He tried loftily dismissing this altered view of his attachment to Mrs. Boye as provincial and Philistine, but achieved nothing. Without his consciously choosing it, the word “Bohemian” rose to express a distaste no reasoning could remove. Accordingly, once he had secured his old lodgings on the embankment, he paid his first call to the Neergaards instead of Mrs. Boye.
He went to see her the next day, but she was out. The janitor told him she had rented a villa at Emiliekilde. Niels was surprised: he knew her father's country place stood in that same neighbourhood.
Well, in a day or two he would make the journey out.

The very next morning, however, a note arrived from Mrs. Boye, asking him to see her at her town apartment. Her pale niece had noticed him in the street. He was to arrive at a quarter to one; he _must_ be there. She would explain the reason, _unless he already knew_. Did he know? He mustn't think badly of her, or behave unreasonably. He knew her far too well: why should he respond like someone with a vulgar soul? Please, he mustn't! They were different from other people, after all. If only he _would_ try to understand! Niels, Niels!

The note threw him into an odd agitation. Uneasily he recalled Mrs. Neergaard's expression, a mixture of mockery and compassion, and the peculiar significance of her silent smiles. What could the matter be? What on earth had taken place?

The feeling that had made him avoid Mrs. Boye disappeared so completely that he could no longer comprehend having felt it. He was frightened. Why hadn't they written to one another, as any sensible people would! _Why_ had there been no letters? He could hardly claim to have been too busy. How strange that wherever he found himself could absorb him so entirely that he forgot everything at a distance; or, if he remembered, relegated it to some remote background where the present piled over it like mountains. Anyone would suppose he had no imagination at all.

At last he was there! Before he could ring, Mrs. Boye opened the entrance door herself. Without a word she held his hand for a long moment in a sympathetic clasp: the papers had reported his loss. He too remained silent. They passed quietly through the parlour between rows of chairs wearing red-striped covers. Paper covered the chandelier and the panes had been whitewashed. In the sitting-room nothing had changed, save that the Venetian blinds were lowered across the open windows. The faint breeze swayed them, setting up a subdued, regular knocking against the frames. Sunlight reflected from the canal slipped between their yellow slats and threw squares of wavering lines onto the ceiling, trembling in time with the water outside. Apart from that, everything was quiet, motionless, waiting without breathing....

Mrs. Boye seemed unable to choose a seat. Eventually she settled on the rocking-chair and carefully wiped it with her handkerchief; but then she remained behind it, her hands resting on the back. Her gloves were still on. Only one arm had come free of her black, loosely fitted mantilla. She wore silk tartan in a minute check, coordinated with the broad ribbons of her Pamela hat, a wide round shape in pale straw. As she looked down, nervously moving the chair, the brim concealed half her face.
Niels took the piano-stool some way from her, with the air of a man preparing for unwelcome news.
“So you've heard, Niels?”
“I haven't. What am I supposed to have heard?”
She stopped rocking the chair. “I'm engaged.”
“Engaged? But why—how did—Mrs. Boye?”

“Oh, don't use Mrs. Boye, and please don't start being impossible at once!” She rested against the chair's back, looking a little defiant. “You must realize this isn't particularly agreeable for me, standing here having to explain everything. I'm willing to explain, but you could give me a little help.”
“What are you saying? Is there an engagement or isn't there?”
Looking up, she answered with restrained impatience, “I've told you already: there is.”
“Then perhaps you'll permit me to congratulate you, Mrs. Boye, and offer my warmest thanks for the time we've spent as acquaintances.” He stood up and made several little bows, each one mocking.

“Can you leave me so easily, then, just like that? I've become engaged, so we're finished, and everything between us becomes some silly old tale we mustn't ever remember. What's over is over, and that's that. Niels, all those days we treasured: are their memories to fall silent now? Will you truly never think about me, never miss having me? On quiet evenings, won't you summon our dream and paint it with all the brightness it could have had? Can you stop yourself from loving it into life again in your imagination, allowing it to mature into everything it might have become? Can you do that? Can you stamp on it and wipe it out completely, every last fragment? Niels!”

“I certainly hope I can. You've proved that it's possible. But all this is absurd, utterly absurd, from first to last. Why stage this little performance? I haven't the faintest right to accuse you. You never loved me and never claimed you did. You allowed me to love you, nothing more; now you're revoking the permission. Unless you mean to let me continue, even though you've committed yourself to someone else? If you think that possible, I can't understand you. Neither of us is a child. Or do you worry I'll forget you too quickly? Don't be concerned: a woman like you isn't easily erased from a man's life. But be careful! No woman receives love such as mine twice in her lifetime; be careful that rejecting me doesn't bring you sorrow! I wish you no harm, none at all! May illness and poverty never touch you. May you enjoy every happiness that money, admiration, and success in society can offer, in the fullest, most overflowing measure: that is what I wish you. May the entire world open before you, except for one small door, a single little door that stays shut however hard you knock or struggle with it. Otherwise, may everything open as completely and generously as anyone could desire.”

His words came slowly, almost sorrowfully, without bitterness. His voice carried an unfamiliar, strangely vibrating note, and it touched her. A little pale now, she leaned rigidly against the chair. “Niels,” she said, “don't prophesy unhappiness! You must remember you weren't here. And my love—I hadn't understood how genuine it was. I took it for something that merely interested me. It moved through my days like a lovely poem of the spirit; it never seized me with strong arms. It had wings, nothing but wings, or so I believed. Only now do I know otherwise, or rather, I knew the instant I'd done it, said yes, and everything. It was all so complicated, so much happening together, so many people to think about.... My brother started it, Hardenskjold, the one who'd been in the West Indies, remember? At home he had been rather wild. Out there he steadied himself and turned thoroughly sensible, joined someone in business and earned a fortune, and married a wealthy widow, a dear little creature, really. He and Father were reconciled, because Hardie had changed so much. Oh, you can't imagine his respectability now, or how much he cares what everyone says—so terribly bourgeois, oh! Naturally he wanted me restored to the family circle. Whenever he visited he argued and preached and coaxed, and Father is getting old, you know. Finally I gave in, and everything went back to how it used to be.”
She paused for a brief moment to remove her mantilla, then her hat and gloves. Occupied with taking all these things off, she turned slightly away from Niels and continued speaking.

“Then there was Hardie's friend, such a respected man—oh, extraordinarily respected. Everyone urged me to accept him; they wanted it so much. And, you see, I could regain my place in society, a better place, really, since he is held in such high esteem in every respect. After all, I've wanted that for quite some time. You can't understand, I suppose? You'd never have expected it of me? You expected exactly the opposite, because I was always laughing at respectable society, its trite opinions, its ready-made morality, its virtue thermometer and its womanliness compass. Remember how clever we thought ourselves! It makes one want to cry, Niels: it wasn't honest, or wasn't always. Let me tell you something. We women can escape for a little while, when some event has awakened us to the desire for freedom that does exist inside us; but we can't sustain it. That appetite for absolute propriety, for the highest refinement right up to its most scrupulous little point, runs in our blood. We can't bear to be fighting the established arrangements that ordinary people all accept. Deep down we actually believe they're right, because they're the people who pass judgment. Whatever bold face we put on, inwardly we submit to their verdicts and suffer under them. Being exceptional doesn't come naturally to women, Niels, truly. It makes us so peculiar, perhaps more fascinating, but still—do you see what I mean? Foolish, isn't it? Surely, though, you can understand how strangely it affected me to find myself in the old surroundings. So much returned, memories of Mother, of the values she'd held. I felt I'd sailed back into a sheltered harbour. Everything was calm and orderly; I had only to attach myself to it and I could live in proper happiness ever afterwards. So I let them fasten the bonds, Niels.”

Niels couldn't suppress a smile. He felt so much above her, and pitied her so much, standing there as miserably as a schoolgirl amid all her admissions. His feelings softened; no harsh words came to him.
He crossed the room towards her.

She had meanwhile pulled the chair round and lowered herself into it. Now she reclined there, looking abandoned and touching, her arms dangling and her face tilted upward. Through half-closed eyes she stared past the two ranks of chairs in the darkened parlour towards the dim entrance hall.
Bending over her, Niels stretched his arm across the chair's back and placed his hand on its armrest. “And you'd forgotten all about—me?” he murmured.
She gave no sign of hearing; her eyes did not even rise. Finally she made the smallest movement of her head, saying no. After another lengthy pause she repeated it, just as faintly.

At first the rooms around them lay utterly quiet. Then a maid went noisily along the passages, singing as she polished the door fittings. The rattle of handles turning brutally broke the hush, so that when it suddenly returned it seemed still deeper. Eventually only the blinds could be heard, their sleepy tapping always the same.

The hush appeared to take away their ability to speak, almost their ability to think. She remained seated, staring into the dim hall. He stayed bent above her, studying the design of her silk gown. Without knowing what he was doing, drawn into the surrounding quiet, he started the chair rocking: very—gently—very—gently....

She raised her lids to glance at his profile in shadow, then let them fall, peacefully satisfied. It felt like an embrace that went on and on. As the chair tilted backward she seemed to surrender into his arms; as it swung forward and her feet met the floor, the pressure of the boards on her soles carried something of him. He sensed it as well, and began attending to the motion, making the rocking stronger. The farther back he drew the chair, the closer he seemed to come to possessing her. At the instant before its forward plunge there was expectation; when it descended, the gentle sound of her unresisting feet touching down gave a peculiar satisfaction. Then he pressed the chair a little farther, softly pushing her sole into the boards and making her knee lift the smallest amount. In that movement there was complete possession.
Finally Niels sighed and let the chair go. “We must stop dreaming!”
“No, let's dream!” Her voice was almost a plea, and her wide, yearning eyes met his with an innocent look.
She rose from the chair gradually.

“Enough of dreams!” Niels said uneasily, slipping an arm about her waist. “There have been far too many between us already. Didn't you ever sense them? Didn't they brush against you, like a gentle breath against your face, or fingers moving your hair? Can the night really never have trembled with sighs, one after another, settling on your lips and dying there?”
He kissed her. Beneath his kisses she seemed to lose her youth a little, yet grew more beautiful: less young, but with a warmer radiance, a more enticing beauty.
“You have to understand,” he said. “You don't know my love for you, or what yearning and pain I've endured. Oh, if only my rooms on the embankment had a voice, Tema!”

He covered her with kisses, and she flung her arms around his neck so recklessly that her broad silk sleeves slid back past the swelling lace of her white undersleeves, past the grey elastic that gathered them above her elbows.
“What would your rooms tell me, Niels?”
“They'd say Tema, ten thousand times and still more. They'd plead in that name and rage in it, sigh in it and sob in it; they could even utter threats against Tema.”
“Really, could they?”

A conversation rose from the road below and entered through the open window, not a word missing. Two unexcitable, gossiping voices joined together the most ordinary worldly advice, lazily delivered in exhausted phrases. Their very prosaicness made it more marvellous to stand here with their hearts together, protected by the gentle half-light.

“How much I love you, my darling, my darling. Holding you, I find you so precious; are you so precious, so very precious? And your hair—I can scarcely get words out, and all those memories of mine—so precious—all the memories of my misery and my tears, of that dreadful yearning, are crowding in and forcing a place for themselves, as though they wanted a share in my happiness, wanted to be happy too. Do you understand? Remember last year's moonlight, Tema? Do you like moonlight? Oh, you've no idea how pitiless it can be. On a clear moonlit night the air seems frozen solid with cold brightness, and the clouds stretch in long layers. Tema, leaves and blossoms keep their perfume drawn so tightly round them that it lies like scented frost. Every sound seems distant and dies so abruptly, without lingering. Such nights have no mercy: they sharpen longing to an extraordinary intensity. The stillness pulls it from every hidden place in your soul, sucks it out with cruel lips. And through all that clarity there's no spark of hope, no sleeping promise. Oh, how I wept, Tema! Have you never wept through a night of moonlight? Darling, it would be a crime to make you cry. You must never cry; you must have nothing but sunshine and nights filled with roses, a night filled with roses—”

She yielded completely to his arms. Her eyes disappeared into his gaze, and her mouth murmured words of love of a strange sweetness, softened almost to silence by her breathing. They were his own words repeated, as though she were whispering them inward to her heart.

When the voices below stopped, she moved uneasily. Soon they sounded again, accompanied by the steady, firm beat of a walking stick on the paving stones. They crossed the street, lingered for a long while farther away, diminished to a low murmur, and vanished.

Once more the silence rose about them, flaring around them, alive with pounding hearts, warm and heavy with breathing, pliant. Words seemed burned away between them. Long kisses passed from mouth to mouth, laden with questions neither spoke, bringing neither comfort nor happiness in the present moment. Their eyes held one another's, afraid to turn aside, but equally afraid to let a message appear in the look. Instead they drew a veil across it, retreating behind their gaze and hiding in silence, absorbed in dreams they kept concealed.
A tremor ran through the arms that held her, rousing her. With both hands she pushed him away and released herself.
“Leave, Niels, leave! You can't stay here, you can't. Are you listening?”

He attempted to pull her close again. She escaped him, frantic and white-faced, shaking all over. She stood with her arms stretched away from her sides, as though she feared the touch of her own body.
Niels moved to kneel down and take her hand.

“Keep your hands off me!” Her eyes were desperate. “Why won't you leave when I'm pleading with you? For heaven's sake, why can't you just go? No, no, don't say anything, leave me, you—can't you see how I tremble in front of you? Look at me, look! Oh, how wickedly you're behaving towards me! And I keep begging you to leave!”
There was no chance to utter a word; she refused to hear him. She had lost all command of herself. Tears poured out; her features were nearly contorted, and her face was so pale it seemed luminous.

“Oh, leave me! Don't you understand that staying here degrades me? You're being cruel, that's what you're doing! How have I wronged you, that you should treat me this way? Please go! Haven't you any compassion?”

Compassion? Rage had turned him cold. The whole thing was insane! Nevertheless he could only leave, and leave he did. He disliked those two files of chairs, but he passed slowly between them, staring straight at them in deliberate defiance.
“Exit Niels Lyhne,” he remarked as the entrance door's latch clicked shut at his back.

With his hat in his hand he descended the stairs, thinking. At the landing he halted and began gesturing to himself. If only he understood a single part of it! Why had _this_ happened, and then why _that_? He went down again. There were her open windows. He wanted to rip apart the sugary, sickening quiet up there with a piercing shout. He wanted someone to talk at for hours, without mercy, pouring foolishness into that stillness until cold nonsense washed it clean. It stayed in his blood: he could see it, taste it, was walking inside it. Suddenly he stopped, flushing scarlet with furious humiliation. Had she made him a means of tempting herself?

Upstairs Mrs. Boye continued to cry. She had moved to the tall mirror and leaned both hands on the table beneath it. Tears dropped from her cheeks into the pink hollow of a great seashell on the table. Above the patch her breath had clouded on the glass she watched her own twisted face. She followed each tear as it brimmed over her eyelid and travelled down. Where could so many come from? She had never wept this way before—except once, at Frascati, after a runaway.
After a time the tears slowed, though an uncontrollable nervous shudder still passed through her intermittently, from her neck right down to her heels.

Sunlight now struck the glass head-on. The rippling reflections from the water slanted across the space beneath the ceiling. Along the edges of the blinds, parallel beams arranged themselves in rows, like neat shelves of yellow light. The room grew hotter. Other smells began mixing with the rich odour of heated wood and dust warmed by the sun: scents drifted from the brilliant flowers on the cushions, the curved silk backs of chairs, the books and folded rugs. Heat freed a hundred perfumes long forgotten there and sent them floating through the room, weightless as ghosts.

Very gradually the shaking stopped. In its place came an odd light-headedness, where fanciful feelings, more than half physical sensations, wheeled along the paths of her astonished thoughts. She shut her eyes, still facing her reflection, and did not move.

How strange, the way that piercing fear had seized her! Had she screamed aloud? A cry seemed to echo in her ears; her throat felt strained, as though she had given a long shriek of anguish. Suppose he had taken her! She let herself be taken, while folding her arms over her breast as if to defend herself. She resisted, and yet—now she seemed to fall naked through the air, flushed, burning with shame, while every wind in heaven touched her shamelessly. He refused to leave, and soon it would be too late. Her strength was escaping in bursting bubbles; one after another they pressed through her lips and broke without stopping. A second more and it would be too late! Had she gone down on her knees to beg him? Too late! Nothing could prevent her rising into his arms, like a bubble ascending through water. Trembling, her soul rose naked before him, every desire exposed, every private dream and concealed surrender laid open to his commanding gaze. In his embrace again, lingering there, deliciously shivering. She saw an alabaster figure encircled by fire, glowing translucent in the flames. Gradually the darkness at its core dissolved, until nothing remained but shining light.

She slowly lifted her eyelids and gave the woman in the mirror a guarded smile, as one smiles at an accomplice without wishing to reveal quite everything. Then she walked around collecting her hat, her gloves, and her mantilla.

The faintness had vanished as though swept off by wind; only a rather agreeable weakness lingered in her knees. She paced about to savour it. Passing the rocking-chair, she secretly nudged it with her elbow, an intimate little greeting disguised as accident.
She rather enjoyed a dramatic scene.
Her glance bade farewell to something no one could see. Then she raised the blinds, and the room seemed transformed into another place.

Three weeks afterward Mrs. Boye married, leaving Niels Lyhne entirely to his own company. He found it difficult to sustain his outrage at the undignified eagerness with which she had rushed back to the conventional world she had mocked so often. Certainly, it had only to open its door and beckon, and there she was. But he could scarcely cast stones: hadn't honest bourgeois respectability exerted its pull on him too? If only that final encounter had never happened! Suppose she really had done what he accused her of doing; suppose it had been a reckless leave-taking of her former life, one final wanton escapade before her retreat into “the quintessence of propriety”—was it possible? What limitless contempt for herself, what cynical ridicule of him and of herself and of everything they had held together, their recollections and expectations, their ardour and their sacred beliefs! He alternated between burning shame and fury. Yet was he treating her justly? Perhaps she had simply spoken openly and honestly: These things are drawing me towards the other camp, drawing me strongly; nevertheless I acknowledge your claim more completely than you yourself demand, and here I stand. If you can possess me, I belong to you; otherwise I follow the stronger force. If that was the truth, hadn't she acted entirely within her rights? He had failed to possess her. The last choice _might_ turn on something so slight, the shade of a thought, a mood's smallest tremor.

If only he could know what she must have known for a moment, and had probably ceased to know already! He hated believing the charge he couldn't stop making against her. For her sake, yes, but still more for his own: somehow it seemed to stain his own shield of honour. Not by any logic, certainly, and yet—

However she had left him, one fact remained: he was alone. At first he felt the vacancy, but before long he also felt relief. There was so much awaiting him. The year spent at Lönborggaard and abroad had filled his thoughts, yet in another sense had been a rest imposed upon him. That interval had sharpened his understanding of his own capabilities and limits, and this very clarity urged him to exercise his gifts in uninterrupted labour. He had no immediate eagerness to create; he wanted to gather. The material he longed to master was so inexhaustible that he began thinking sadly about the shortness of human life. He had never squandered his hours; still, freeing oneself from one's father's bookshelf is difficult. Following roads on which others have reached their destination appears the easiest way to arrive. So, instead of searching the enormous realm of books for a Vineland of his own, he had travelled where his forefathers pointed. Dutifully he had refused to look at many tempting things, hoping to see better in the immense darkness of the Eddas and sagas. He had stopped his ears against many voices inviting him, hoping to hear more distinctly the mysterious speech of nature in folk songs.

Now, at last, he realized that no natural law required him to be either Romantic or Old Norse. Speaking his own doubts directly was simpler than attributing them to Gorm, the worshipper of Loki. Giving language to the secret movements within himself made more sense than shouting at the monastery walls of the Middle Ages and receiving his own voice back as a remote echo.

His mind had always welcomed the fresh thinking of his age. But he had busied himself tracing anticipations of the New in the Old, instead of attending to the New's clear, direct account of itself. There was nothing unusual about him in that respect: no new gospel has ever been announced without setting the whole world rummaging among the ancient prophets.

That no longer satisfied him. With ardour Niels launched himself into his new work. He felt the desire to conquer, the hunger for the power knowledge brings, which surely visits everyone labouring in the realm of thought at least once, if only for a fleeting hour, however humble a drudge that person later becomes. Those of us whom fortune has allowed to cultivate our minds—which of us has never gazed in delight over learning's endless sea? Which of us has not approached its clear, cold water and, with youth's cheerful presumption, started emptying it with cupped hands, like the child in the legend? Remember how the sun might laugh over a lovely summer landscape, while you noticed neither blossoms nor sky nor running stream? Life's festivals passed without stirring even a dream in your youthful blood, and your own home seemed distant: do you remember? Remember too how, out of the yellow pages, a building took shape within your thoughts, whole and finished, resting in itself like a work of art. Every detail was yours, and your spirit inhabited it. The columns rose slenderly, their daring curves aware of their own strength; the bold upward striving was yours, and yours the courage that sustained the load. The vaulted ceiling seemed to hover, having gathered its whole weight, stone on stone, into massive drops and set them on the columns' necks. That dream of floating without weight came from you; so did the arches' confident downward thrust. It was you, setting your foot upon what belonged to you.

Through knowledge your character grows in this way, gaining clarity and becoming whole. Learning has a beauty equal to living. Don't fear losing yourself inside a mind greater than your own! Don't anxiously brood over your individuality, or bar yourself against influences that powerfully attract you, afraid their strong current will carry you away and drown those cherished little peculiarities of your inner self! There is nothing to fear! Whatever individuality can disappear in the sorting and remaking of healthy growth is only a defect: a shoot raised without light, remarkable only while it keeps its sickly colour. What is healthy and growing within you is what you must live by. Greatness can grow only from health.

Christmas Eve arrived before Niels Lyhne had noticed it approaching. For six months he had seen nobody socially except the Neergaards, and them only occasionally. They asked him to join them that evening. But the Christmas Eve before had been that unforgettable evening in Clarens, so he chose solitude.

A strong wind was blowing. A light snowfall covered the roads, still untrampled into sludge, making them look broader. White on rooftops and ledges lent the houses a certain loveliness while also making each seem more alone. The lamps fluttered in the wind. Every so often, as though distracted, one flung a spot of brightness onto a wall, rousing a shopkeeper's sign from its reverie and making its great letters stare blankly out. The shop windows, only partly illuminated and still in disorder after the Christmas trade, looked unfamiliar too, curiously lost in thought.

He entered the smaller streets, where festivities appeared well under way. Music issued from cellars and low-ceilinged rooms, a fiddle here and there, more often a barrel organ grinding out dancing tunes. Something about the musicians' earnest goodwill suggested the agreeable exertion of dancing more than its festive enchantment. One imagined dragging feet and air thick with bodily heat. Or so it struck the solitary man outside, whose loneliness turned him into a critic of all this companionship. He felt much closer to the labourer standing with his child before a tiny shop, debating some inexpensive wonder in its faintly lit display, clearly determined to settle their choice before entering that cave of temptations. He felt for the shabby elderly gentlewomen too, passing singly, almost one at every hundred paces. They wore the oddest coats and mantillas, survivors of forgotten fashions; their old necks moved with timid, mistrustful jerks, like wary birds. They walked uncertainly, hesitantly, as people long out of practice with the world: as though, day after day, they had sat forgotten in secret corners of rear apartments and attic lodgings, and only on this one night of the year were they remembered and invited out. The thought saddened him. His heart contracted with a sick feeling as he tried to imagine the life of one such solitary old unmarried woman, slowly dripping away. In his ears a clock on a mantel seemed to tick with painful regularity, “once-again, once-again,” letting the empty seconds fall separately into the day's chalice until it brimmed.

Well, this Christmas meal had to be dealt with. He went back the way he had come, dimly afraid that different streets would expose him to further species of lonely people, fresh varieties of abandonment. Those he had already met had left enough bitterness in his mouth.

In the broader streets he could breathe more easily. He stepped out faster, a little defiantly, separating himself inwardly from the scenes he had passed by reminding himself that his own solitude was a choice.

He went into one of the larger restaurants. Waiting for his meal, he watched arrivals from behind an old newspaper supplement. They were mostly young men. A few looked defiant, as if warning everyone present against claiming them as companions in misery. Others could hardly hide their embarrassment at having nowhere else to be that evening. All favoured remote corners and tables apart. Many arrived in pairs, and the greater number of those pairs were plainly brothers; Niels had never encountered so many brothers in one place. Their clothes and manners often differed greatly, and their hands showed the differences in their circumstances still more distinctly. Any real closeness between them seemed rare, whether as they entered or after sitting and conversing awhile. Here one assumed superiority and the other admiration; there one offered warmth and the other resisted. Some watched each other warily, or, worse, silently condemned each other's purposes, ambitions, and ways of pursuing them. Evidently most required both a holiday and a measure of loneliness before they remembered their shared beginnings and sought one another out.

Reflecting on this, Niels marvelled at everyone's patience. Nobody rang a bell or summoned a waiter, as though by unspoken agreement they wanted to remove as much of the restaurant character from the room as they could. In the midst of these thoughts he noticed an acquaintance just entering. A known face appearing suddenly among all those strangers startled him; he stood and went to greet the man with a pleased, if rather surprised, “Good evening.”
“Are you expecting someone?” the man asked, seeking somewhere to put his overcoat.
“No, just myself.”
“Then that's fortunate for me!”

The arrival was Dr. Hjerrild, a young man Niels had encountered at the Neergaards. From hints dropped by Mrs. Neergaard, rather than any remark of his own, Niels knew his religious opinions were extremely liberal, although the political views he declared were precisely the opposite. Such people seldom visited the Neergaards, who combined liberal politics with religious faith. Through his late mother's influence, as well as his own tastes, the doctor belonged to one of the circles quite common then where people greeted the new liberal doctrines sceptically, even antagonistically. On religious questions, unless mysticism or indifference claimed them, they went somewhat beyond rationalism while stopping somewhat short of atheism. These circles contained many gradations of belief. Broadly, though, they agreed that Holstein lay at least as close to their affections as Slesvig. They paid no attention to the relationship with Sweden and were not wholly favourable to the newest forms of Danism. They also knew Molière more intimately than Holberg, and Baggesen more intimately than Oehlenschläger; their preferences in art perhaps leaned towards sentimentality.

These, or similar, had been the influences forming Hjerrild. He regarded Niels with some doubt while Niels described what he had noticed among the diners, especially their evident embarrassment at belonging to no home, or even an imitation of home, on this particular evening.

“That's quite understandable,” he answered coldly, almost brushing him off. “Nobody chooses a restaurant on Christmas Eve for pleasure. Being excluded must inevitably feel humiliating, whether other people caused it or they did themselves. May I ask what brings you here? You needn't answer if you'd prefer not to.”
Niels explained that he was there simply because he had spent the previous Christmas Eve with his mother, and she was now dead.

“Forgive me,” Hjerrild said. “You were kind to tell me, and I owe you an apology for my distrust. You see, I could easily picture you coming here to give the institution of Christmas a young man's defiant kick. My own reason, though, is precisely consideration for other people's Christmas. Since coming to this city, I've always spent Christmas Eve with an exceptionally kind family from my home town, until tonight. Somehow I began to feel I was an intrusion when they sang their carols. Not that they were embarrassed; they're too strong-minded for that. But having someone present for whom the hymns might as well be sung into a void made them uncomfortable. So I imagined, at any rate.”

They ate the rest of their dinner with little talk, lit cigars, and decided to find their toddy elsewhere. Tonight neither wanted to stare at the same red couches and gilt mirror frames that faced them on so many other evenings throughout the year. They took refuge instead in a small café they rarely visited.
They quickly saw they could not comfortably remain there.

At the back, the proprietor and waiters were playing loo with two trumps, together with several friends. The proprietor's wife and daughters watched and served refreshments, though they did not serve the newcomers; a waiter attended to them. The two drank quickly, aware that their arrival had disturbed the gathering. Conversation quietened, and the proprietor, previously in shirtsleeves, looked awkward and pulled on his jacket.
Walking along the street again, Niels remarked, “We do seem short of a home this evening.”
“Well, that's only fitting,” Hjerrild replied, with a rather melancholy air.
Christianity became their subject of conversation; the topic seemed to be everywhere around them.
Niels attacked Christianity passionately, though his arguments remained fairly broad.

Hjerrild tired of covering once more the familiar ground of arguments he had heard before. Abruptly, without much connection to the preceding talk, he said, “Be careful, Lyhne. Christianity holds the throne. Fighting the truth that reigns in the name of a truth that is merely heir apparent is foolish.”
“Foolish or wise—why should that make a difference?”

“Don't dismiss it quite so readily. I wasn't offering the banal observation that it is foolish in worldly terms. It is foolish morally as well, and worse than foolish. Be cautious about committing yourself too completely to this particular current of our age, unless your own nature absolutely requires it. Surely a poet has plenty of other concerns.”
“I don't follow you. I can't regard myself as a hurdy-gurdy, removing a piece nobody likes and replacing it with whatever tune is on everybody's lips.”

“Can't you? Plenty of people manage it. At least you can announce, ‘We're not playing that piece at the moment.’ We often have more capacity in that direction than we suppose. A person isn't such an inseparable whole. Exercise your right arm fiercely and continually, and blood flows into it; it grows at the rest of the body's expense. Meanwhile your legs, which you're sparing as much as possible, naturally grow somewhat thinner. You can work out the analogy. Have you observed that most of our country's idealistic energies, probably its finest ones, are devoted entirely to political liberty? There is something to learn there. Believe me, working for an idea that advances has a redeeming power. Belonging to a defeated minority, on the other hand, can profoundly corrupt a person, as life's inexorable progress proves it wrong at every point and every step. How could the effect be otherwise? It is bitterly dispiriting to watch what your deepest self knows as right and true—Truth herself—insulted and slapped by the lowest hanger-on of the victorious army. You hear her abused, and can do nothing except love her with greater faithfulness, kneel inwardly before her with still more devotion, and continue to see her lovely face as lovely and majestic as before. Its immortal radiance persists, however much dust blows round her white brow, however thick the poisonous mist gathering about her halo. It is terribly dispiriting, and damage to the soul is inevitable. How easy to hate until the heart is exhausted, to wrap yourself in contempt's cold shade, or let pain numb you and abandon the world to its own course. Unless, of course, you possess _something_ that prevents you from choosing comfort or evading the question altogether: something that keeps you upright, every faculty alert, every sympathy awake, accepting defeat's wounds and jabs as the lash strikes your back over and over. And still you hold your bleeding hope upright, listening for remote thunder that foretells upheaval, watching for a far, faint sunrise that one day, at some time, perhaps.... If that _something_ lives in you! But don't attempt it, Lyhne. Consider the existence such a man must lead if he remains faithful to himself. He cannot speak a word without knowing that ridicule and contempt await everything he says! His words are twisted, dirtied, pulled apart, made into clever traps for his own feet; before he can recover them from the mire and set them straight, the whole world has suddenly lost its hearing. Then he starts afresh somewhere else, and it happens again, and again. Perhaps worst of all, honourable women and men misunderstand and despise him, people he himself admires and respects despite their opposing convictions. Yet that is inevitable; it cannot happen differently. The opposition must expect attack not for its actual character or actual aims, but for whatever character and aims the ruling party chooses to assign it. Besides, exercising power over the weaker means abusing it; what other outcome is possible? Surely nobody expects those in power to surrender their advantages so that their opponents can meet them evenly. That truth does not make the opposition's battle any less agonizing or less likely to break the heart. With all this in mind, Lyhne, can you seriously believe anyone could fight on with so many vultures' beaks sunk in his body, unless he possessed the blind, obstinate ardour we call fanaticism? And how can anyone become fanatical over a denial? Fanatical over the claim that God doesn't exist! Yet victory requires fanaticism. Quiet now, listen!”
They halted outside a house whose raised curtain revealed a spacious room. From the window, open just a little, the clear voices of children and women carried a song down to them:
“_A child is born in Bethlehem, In Bethlehem. Therefore rejoice, Jerusalem! Hallelujah, Hallelujah!_”
They continued without speaking. Along the hushed road the singing followed them, and the piano notes followed still more distinctly.

“Did you catch that?” Hjerrild asked. “Could you hear the ardour in that ancient Hebrew cry of victory? And those names of two Jewish towns! Jerusalem meant more than a symbol: the whole city, Copenhagen, Denmark; it meant _Us_, the Christian nation inside the nation.”
“There is no God, and man is his prophet,” Niels answered, with bitterness and a certain sadness.

“Precisely,” Hjerrild said mockingly. “When all is said, atheism is indescribably flat. What does it finally aim at except a humanity stripped of illusion? The belief that a God governs everything and judges everything is our last magnificent illusion. Once it disappears, what remains? You're wiser, certainly; but are you happier, are you richer? I don't see how.”

“Can't you see,” Niels Lyhne cried, “that when people can freely rejoice and declare, ‘There is no God!’ that very day will conjure a new earth and a new heaven? Only then will heaven become open, limitless space, instead of an eye that watches and threatens. Once that dim afterworld of punishment or bliss bursts like a bubble, the earth will belong to us, and we to the earth. This earth will be our real homeland, our hearts' home, where we live for our entire time, instead of passing briefly as strangers and travellers. Imagine how concentrated life will become when all of it must be lived here and nothing can be reserved for an afterlife. The enormous river of love now flowing upward to the God people believe in will turn back towards the earth. It will flow affectionately among all those fine human qualities we bestowed on the divine, adorning it so that it would deserve our love: kindness, justice, wisdom—who could list them all? Think of the dignity people will gain when they can live their own lives and die their own deaths without terror of hell or expectation of heaven, looking to themselves for hope and fearing their own judgment. Think how their consciences will develop, how strong they will become, when helpless remorse and humility no longer make amends, when forgiveness can be earned only by undoing through good the evil they committed.”
“Your confidence in human beings must be extraordinary. In that case, atheism will ask more of them than Christianity ever has.”
“Naturally it will!”
“Naturally; but where do you propose to find all the strong people your society of atheists will require?”

“Gradually. Atheism must produce them itself. I know perfectly well that this generation isn't ready, nor the next, nor the one after it. But each generation will contain a handful who sincerely try to live and die by it, and succeed. In time they will become a line of spiritual forebears, giving their descendants a source of courage and a past to remember proudly. The early years will be the hardest. Many will be defeated; even the victors will carry ragged flags, because tradition will still saturate their very marrow. Convincing the intellect isn't enough: blood and nerves must be convinced, wishes and hopes, even the dreams we dream! But that doesn't matter. Eventually the day will arrive, and the handful will have grown into the multitude.”
“Do you believe so? I'm searching for a term. Would pietistical atheism serve?”
Niels began, “Every genuine atheism—” but Hjerrild interrupted him.
“Naturally,” he said, “naturally! Certainly, give us just one entrance, a single needle's eye through which every camel on earth must pass.”
